items.title: Cloudflare releases weights of Clairic, its AI that reads invoices and receipts
items.story_key: story|title:cloudflare releases weights of clairic its ai that reads invoices and receipts
items.content_excerpt: Cloudflare released the weights of Clairic and Clairic-flash, two Apache 2.0 models that extract data from documents, with scores it measured itself. On November 18, 2026, Cloudflare made two of its AI models free to download. Called Clairic and Clairic-flash, they pull data out of documents such as invoices and receipts. A company can now run these models locally , on its own servers, without sending its documents to an online service. Both models read a block of text, a photo or a PDF page. They pick out specific pieces of information, such as a supplier’s name, a total amount or a date. Cloudflare is the US company best known for the network that protects and speeds up websites. It released both models under Apache 2.0, an open-source license that allows commercial use and modification. The release covers the models’ weights. These are the billions of numbers, called parameters, that a model learns during training. Clairic has 27 billion parameters and Clairic-flash has 9 billion. Cloudflare still sells both as a paid service on Workers AI, its platform for running AI models on its own network. Both models work by filling in a form. They receive a document and a list of fields, and each field has a set type: text, number, date, duration, list, estimate or forecast. For each field, they return one value plus a confidence score that says how sure the model is. When the value appears word for word in the document, they also give its exact position. Cloudflare files these models under a category it calls “System One,” named after the fast mode of thinking described by psychologist Daniel Kahneman. Cloudflare credits the idea to TypeSafe, a company whose Jev model was built for one specific job and priced low. Cloudflare says its models of this kind usually answer in under a second. By its account, a large language model, the general-purpose kind of AI behind chatbots, takes several seconds to reason through the same step. Cloudflare first showed Clairic on October 19, 2026, as a preview: a test version available only as an online service. The announcement said Cloudflare intended to release the weights “soon.” The October post also explained the name: Clairic partly comes from “clair,” the French word for “clear,” as in “Clair de lune.” Cloudflare said the model is meant to extract data clearly and keep the books accurate. The versions released on November 18 can read PDFs, which the preview could not. They accept up to four images or PDF pages per request.

items.story_key: story|title:llm call is doing more than you think
items.content_excerpt: Audiala replaced an LLM router with a decision model and rolled it back 23 minutes later. The replacement could classify intent. The incumbent also resolved cities, conversational references, and tool-control flags. The team had evaluated one responsibility and replaced several. The migration account was one of the clearest examples in Part 1, our survey of decision-model adoption . Other integrations exposed related problems: candidate construction constrained action selection, missing handoff instructions weakened downstream agents, and faster decisions sometimes produced more recovery work. Those reports describe particular implementations, not a universal penalty for specialization. They do suggest a practical starting point: the unit of replacement is the behavior the application depends on. This article follows that idea into the implementation. We will recover a call's contract, construct alternatives, evaluate the complete replacement, and account for keeping it reliable. It appears to select a vendor. But which entity counts as the vendor: the issuing legal entity, a trading name, or the parent company? What happens when two catalog entries share a name? Does a tax identifier override the letterhead? Can the function return an entity absent from the catalog? Does a successful result merely populate a review screen, or does downstream code use it to choose a payment destination? The original prompt may have absorbed several of those responsibilities. It might interpret the invoice, reconcile conflicting evidence, identify an entity, and explain uncertainty in a field the next step reads. A replacement that returns a valid identifier can still lose behavior the application needs. Start with the consumers. Inspect field access, database lookups, tool arguments, intermediate messages, and recovery paths. Read the prompt alongside those dependencies. A field ignored by the immediate caller may still become evidence in a later model call. Conversely, a requested explanation nobody consumes may not belong in the required output. Part 1's LAS case makes this concrete: planners supplied handoff instructions, and reviewers supplied repair guidance. items.title: Safe to Omit, Worth Omitting? Keeping the Answer and Cutting Latency When an LLM Agent Skips Another's Message
items.summary: In multi-agent systems, a receiver agent often waits for a helper agent's message (text or its latent KV cache), which can improve performance but adds latency. We study when a receiver agent can skip the message safely (the final answer rarely changes) and beneficially (the time saved exceeds the cost of deciding). Our mechanism reads the receiver agent's confidence without the message and uses a finite-sample test to certify a threshold at which, with high probability, at most 5% of skipped answers change; if none passes, the system keeps communicating. We test it on OpenBookQA, ARC-Challenge, and MMLU-Pro with three Qwen model pairs, on cross-family agents, and on SQuAD and GSM8K. Four insights emerge. First, oracle headroom is weak evidence that messages help: control inputs without answer-specific content, matched to change answers as often as real messages, reproduce a median 76% of the oracle's gain. Second, whether a message can be skipped depends on how often and how predictably it alters the answer, not on its accuracy; every certified KV-cache path is less accurate than the receiver agent alone. Third, where text messages help, skipping keeps most of their gain: on unseen questions in the four such settings, the policies skip 59 to 80% and keep an estimated 76 to 95% of the gain. In two prospective tests with all rules fixed in advance, our mechanism skips a three-agent system's verifier on 39.9% of sealed questions, keeping 12.55 of its 12.80-point gain, and a 32B helper on 68.4% of held-out questions, keeping its whole gain. Fourth, safety does not determine efficiency: at batch size one, skipping text saves hundreds of milliseconds per query and skipping KV cache far less. Certification extends to SQuAD but not to GSM8K. In eleven tests on unseen questions, every certified policy we could test kept its change rate's 95% upper bound below 5% under our answer parsers.

items.title: Vibe-Trading: Towards Agent-Native Trading
items.summary: Existing AI agents can retrieve information, call tools, run experiments, and produce multi-step outputs. Yet most are built around relatively static workflows and struggle to preserve reliable state as the environment changes. Financial trading makes this limitation especially consequential: prices, news, market conditions, portfolio positions, and available capital evolve continuously. A result is useful only when it remains tied to the correct time, data snapshot, and execution context. We present Vibe-Trading, a comprehensive agent-native trading framework and all-in-one workspace for building, evaluating, and evolving agents for financial trading. It unifies market research, financial data, strategy generation, backtesting, portfolio analysis, paper trading, multi-agent collaboration, and optional broker execution. Its central contribution is an architecture that keeps results, evidence, research history, and trading authority connected throughout the research-to-action process. Each result retains its source, temporal scope, configuration, and producing run. Shared evidence grounding enables verification, versioned research records support reproducible continuation, and an explicit authority gate separates strategy research from live execution. Together, these designs provide a practical foundation for trading agents whose results can be traced, reproduced, and acted on only under explicit authority.

items.title: BaseRSI: Recursive Self-Improvement of a Base Vision-Language Model via Training-Free Harness Internalization
items.summary: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is moving from the harness of prompts and tools around a base model toward the model itself. However, existing RSI still faces key challenges, including harness-bound gains that stay outside the base model, black-box supervision that reads only the model's outputs, and imprecise edits whose site and strength are fixed in advance. To address these challenges, we propose BaseRSI, a new paradigm of Recursive Harness Internalization: the base model improves its harness, then writes what the harness adds into its own weights through training-free edits, round after round on its own responses. To support this paradigm, we introduce ReGap, a mechanism that supervises every transformer block with the high-dimensional activation difference that the harness makes at that block alone, and updates the block's weights along this signal in a low-dimensional subspace. Building on this mechanism, we further propose ReKey, an algorithm that writes this signal by regression into a few key-value neurons of every block, and measures the site and strength of each edit on the model's own responses. Moreover, the base model fills every role of this recursion with forward passes alone, and its edits, written at different sites, compose in one checkpoint without refitting. Experimental results on ten visual reasoning benchmarks show that BaseRSI consistently improves a base vision-language model both in distribution and on held-out benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/beita6969/BaseRSI.

items.title: Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with trained NIST assessors, frontier LLM judges, and recently proposed per-topic classifiers. Our results show that ExecJudges agrees with NIST assessors at the level of the Claude Sonnet 5.5 LLM judges on TREC DL 2019-2021. With a small number of human labels per topic, the ExecJudges-L variant agrees with NIST more than per-topic classifiers with the same labels on all seven collections, and either exceeds the agreement of LLM judges provided the same labels or is within about 0.05 of it in Krippendorff's alpha. The labels rank the official TREC DL runs with Kendall's tau of 0.87 to 0.94, and writing the programs incurs a one-time cost of $0.17 to $0.49 per topic, with no additional costs for grading. Our results suggest that ExecJudges offers a reproducible, inspectable, efficient and cost-effective alternative to LLM judges for labeling deep result pools for system evaluation or ranking improvements.

items.title: vllm v0.34.0
items.summary:
v0.34.0

1,061 commits from 412 contributors (120 new). Thank you!

TL;DR

  • 10 new models (Mistral Large 4, MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, Nemotron-3.5-Transcribe, and more!)
  • Extensible KV cache is on by default: vLLM sizes the KV cache from memory actually free after warmup, so most models get a bigger cache and more throughput - in most cases you should now remove gpu_memory_utilization from your configs.
  • Model Runner V1 is gone. Model Runner V2 is now the only GPU runner.
  • Big speedups on Blackwell and MI355X: up to 1.95× decode (Step5 on GB200), 1.6× throughput (GLM-5.3-Flash), 1.24–1.40× faster long-prompt TTFT (GLM-5.3).
  • Upgrade check: default block size is now 64, ROCm 7.2 images are gone, and huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 is required. See Before you upgrade.

Before you upgrade

Important

These changes can break existing setups.

  • On CUDA and ROCm, the KV cache is sized from memory actually free after CUDA graph capture and warmup, not from an estimate (#56492).
  • Result: a larger cache (e.g. MiniMax-M3 on H200: 433k → 672k tokens), so throughput is higher and TTFT lower at high concurrency.
  • Trade-off: per-token decode latency can rise on some models (TPOT +6–18% on some H200 models at concurrency 128). Opt out with --gpu-memory-utilization 0.9 or --no-enable-extensible-kv-cache.
  • Hardened with fixes for allocator fragmentation, startup OOMs and KV connectors (#67296, #67485, #66731, #66523, #66197, #65137, #66605, #66674).

Model Runner V2 only

  • Model Runner V1 is removed (#63373).
  • Dual-batch overlap now runs on MRV2, including with speculative decoding and DCP (#61464).

Speculative decoding

  • Suffix decoding runs on MRV2 with a GPU speculator; Arctic Inference is no longer needed (#60339).
  • Custom speculators: declarative configs plus a register_speculative_method plugin API (#63205).
  • CUDA graphs for MRV2 draft-model speculators (#60989).
  • Adaptive verification works with XPress (#65175).
  • Draft KV cache matches the target's dtype, so an FP8 target gets an FP8 draft cache (#65198).

    • Dropped with it: the V1 logits-processor API (vllm.v1.worker.gpu.sample.logits_processor is the only interface), the custom_class speculative method, use_heterogeneous_vocab, disable_padded_drafter_batch, parallel_drafting outside DFlash/DSpark, PP with external_launcher, NGramPerReqLogitsProcessor, and x86 CPUs without Triton.
    • Deprecated: parallel_drafting, capture_torch_profiler, enable_layerwise_nvtx_tracing.
  • Default --block-size is 64 instead of 16 (#63231). Backends with a preferred block size still override it (ROCm paged attention keeps 16), and an explicit --block-size still wins.
  • gpu_memory_utilization defaults to 1.0 when unset with the extensible KV cache on (#56492). An explicit value in (0.8, 1.0) that withholds 1 GiB or more logs a warning (#66704).
  • ROCm 7.2 wheels and -rocm72 images are no longer published (#61939).
  • Removed:
    • QuTLASS and the fp_quant method (#65230).
    • Marlin INT8/FP8-activation (W4A8) paths and VLLM_MARLIN_INPUT_DTYPE; use --quantization humming with VLLM_HUMMING_INPUT_QUANT_CONFIG (#65542).
    • Keye-VL and Keye-VL-1.5 (#64287); disable_mtp_completeness_check (#49459); the refresh_derived_weights hook (#65914).
  • Dependencies: huggingface_hub >= 2.0.0 (#64779); mistral-common >= 1.13.0 (#64169); XPU requires vllm_xpu_kernels 0.1.17 (#60609).
  • Model and plugin code: all process_weights_after_loading hooks share one signature and the loader runs every module's hook (#57678); config compute_hash() replaced by compile_factors() / hash_config() (#65652).
  • API behavior:
    • llama3_json no longer streams tool arguments incrementally (#63569).
    • Canary transcription without language returns 400 (#65445).
    • An empty tools array is accepted in both frontends (#65547, #65854).
    • /v1/systemone rejects request-supplied chat templates without --trust-request-chat-template (#64503).
    • LoRA adapters on modules vLLM does not wrap are refused (#63489); misconfigured NCCL weight transfer raises (#57022).
    • vllm-rs serve no longer reads --data-parallel-rank from VLLM_DP_RANK (#65369).
    • AITER fused shared experts with MiniMax M3 and DeepSeek V4 need VLLM_ROCM_USE_AITER=1 (#61457).
  • Still deprecated: --mamba-cache-mode has no effect; its removal was postponed (#64838).
  • New defaults:
    • Extensible KV cache (#56492); block size 64 (#63231); best-effort NUMA binding (#61258).
    • Token-sharded sparse-MLA prefill at 1024 or more prefill tokens (#63956); MLA decode up-projection before the A2A merge (#64994).
    • VLLM_COMPILE_ON_ONE_RANK (#63247); minimum valid EPLB num_redundant_experts (#30614).
    • HiSparse on the extensible KV cache (#65214); encoder CUDA graphs up to encoder_cudagraph_max_token_budget=5120, eager above (#65227).
    • TRITON_ATTN on RDNA3/RDNA4 (#60418); MRV2 on non-Triton CPUs (#61995); float32 Mamba SSM cache for Nemotron Omni (#63218); Zipf routing in vllm bench forward (#64167).

items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added a confirmation before /install-github-app changes a repository
  • Added claude mcp add-json <name> - to read the server's JSON from stdin, so tokens can stay off the command line; not available inside a Claude Code session
  • Added a line when a resumed session's earlier messages can't be loaded
  • Added a list in /status of broken agent, skill, command and output style files, keybinding errors, an unavailable sandbox, ignored permission settings and hook matchers that never match
  • Added a note in /config when other settings override a row
  • Added x-claude-code-managed-settings-checksum to the gateway hint headers; sent where managed settings set CLAUDE_CODE_GATEWAY_HINT_HEADERS=1, including where they already do
  • Added support for naming a session's billing group with the attributionProject setting, for Claude apps gateways that set admin.billing_group_tag
  • Added /tui classic as the name for the non-fullscreen renderer; /tui default still works
  • Remote Control: Fixed stopping the server in worktree mode deleting a running session's git-ignored files, such as .env
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with --use-anthropic-git-proxy deleting a non-empty directory named by GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL at startup: the runner now keeps it, ignores the variable and warns
  • Fixed claude mcp add and claude mcp remove with project scope deleting other top-level keys from .mcp.json, such as $schema or another tool's servers
  • Fixed /export overwriting an existing file without asking: the dialog now asks, and /export <name> keeps the file and says to run /export
  • Fixed a command you had allowed still running after you pressed Stop, when the approval arrived after a restart, in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions with no feature flags loaded
  • Fixed Enter closing /teleport's load error screen
  • Fixed a click followed by Enter in /plugin installing or disabling a plugin
  • Fixed a half-typed ! command running on an extra Enter after the usage limit menu
  • Fixed some --disallowedTools rules with parentheses in their content
  • Fixed auto mode ignoring some wildcard PowerShell allow rules that name a script with .\, such as PowerShell(.\scripts\build.ps1 *)
  • Fixed a running Code Mode script in auto mode getting permission prompts and denials once Claude started a second script that auto mode also allowed
  • Changed some pre-started background sessions to be discarded after an account change
  • Changed a workflow paused at a usage limit in the terminal to stay paused after a login, until the earlier login returns or you type a prompt
  • Fixed a nested claude with its own token being refused by forceLoginOrgUUID: commands that don't get the session's token no longer get its CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_SCOPES; set it on any that need it
  • Fixed headless sessions losing stored messages on resume when a message was sent again with the same UUID after the process was killed
  • Fixed cases where a session resumed after an empty reply or a killed command lost an answer, or brought back a rewound prompt, after another crash or a move to the background
  • Fixed a remote session forgetting messages sent after Stop was pressed during a restart, if Claude Code then crashed
  • Fixed tasks created after /clear being lost, and cleared tasks coming back, when a cloud or self-hosted runner session with no feature flags loaded resumed later
  • Fixed a compaction right after a reply cut at the output token limit losing that reply's tool call and its result
  • Fixed a settings change from /config and similar commands failing to save with no warning; a line under the prompt now says so
  • Fixed /rewind closing without a word when some files could not be restored
  • Fixed pasted images being dropped when the prompt starts with a file path such as /tmp/a.txt
  • Fixed agents passed with --agents being lost once plugins loaded or reloaded
  • Fixed a plugin's agent being dropped when resuming a session from the --resume picker
  • Fixed Claude Code refusing to start when https_proxy or HTTPS_PROXY is a bare host:port and neither its input nor its output is a terminal (the desktop app, an SDK, cron)
  • Fixed Claude Code on Linux sometimes returning to the shell while restarting itself at startup, such as after the first sign-in to a Claude apps gateway or when turning on Code Mode
  • Fixed claude -p hanging before its first request when the fetch of a model's settings stalled, such as at a proxy; it now goes on without them after 10 seconds
  • Fixed the screen staying blank or frozen after a brief out-of-memory error
  • Fixed a rare display fault that could freeze the screen or end the session
  • Fixed cloud sessions breaking when a program left thousands of connections open to the session's network proxy
  • Fixed a turn hanging when a mod's $.model.complete or $.model.classify call met a usage limit: the call now gets the API's error at once; mods should handle that error
  • Fixed stalls on a compaction reply with thousands of unclosed tags and on some very long WebFetch URLs; WebFetch now refuses a URL over 2,000 characters before any permission prompt
  • Fixed a message with thousands of @ mentions stalling before Claude replies; only the first 100 mentions are now looked up as files
  • Fixed the prompt freezing after rejecting a write to a very large file; a rejected write now shows a short preview
  • Fixed a crash when a burst of keys reached the search box in /plugin
  • Fixed a false crash report and exit code when a suspended session resumes, or at exit, where a Linux security policy blocks a process from signalling itself
  • Fixed remote MCP servers staying disconnected after a longer outage such as a VPN drop: most servers on other machines reached by hostname over https are now retried in the background for about a day
  • Fixed Edit refusing with "File has not been read yet" after a compaction on unchanged files outside the project that Claude had already read in full
  • Fixed Grep repeating or skipping results when paging with head_limit and offset; content and count results are now sorted by file path
  • Fixed Read failing on Jupyter notebooks that contain an output of an unknown type
  • Fixed NotebookEdit removing the notebook file's final newline
  • Fixed the Read tool reporting 512KB instead of the real size when a file of 10 MB or more is too large to read at once
  • Fixed the Bash tool's diff of changed files not naming files that are binary, too large or too many to show
  • Fixed artifact publishes failing with "the source file changed between approval and publish" when a synced or remote-backed folder had only changed the file's timestamp
  • Fixed a new artifact that you approved being refused in a cloud scheduled task's session, in organizations that require approval of each new artifact
  • Fixed a new artifact being refused after an app built on the Agent SDK approved it, in organizations that require approval of each new artifact
  • Fixed /artifacts showing part of your list, or "No artifacts yet", when a request for more of the list failed: it now tries again, then warns if it can't load the whole list
  • Fixed in-process agent teammates on a different model from the lead compacting at the lead's context limit and on the wrong model; they now use their own limit and model, at that model's rate
  • Fixed a finished subagent resuming on the model and effort of a sibling subagent that messaged it
  • Fixed the main conversation not being told a background agent had finished when the subagent that started it ended by itself without reading the result, outside auto mode
  • Fixed Claude reporting a background agent as still running when it had waited 30 seconds or more on a permission prompt in the desktop app, on the web and in the SDK
  • Fixed Claude not being told in auto mode when a background agent's reply to a follow-up message was dropped, and reduced repeat wake-ups there from agents waiting on background commands
  • Fixed the desktop app, Claude Code on the web and VS Code showing a raw task notification as a subagent's prompt after its background task woke it
  • Fixed messages sent from another session with "later" priority joining the running turn, instead of waiting for it to end, in Remote Control and Claude Desktop sessions
  • Fixed messages to cloud and Remote Control sessions being reported as failed with a stale address after a timeout or rate limit; Claude now says when a message may have arrived
  • Fixed cloud sessions giving no error when a UserPromptSubmit hook blocks a message sent while Claude works
  • Fixed failing hooks showing nothing: SubagentStop in background agents, SessionEnd at /clear and /resume, and CwdChanged and FileChanged in fullscreen
  • Fixed a Stop hook that failed to run being shown as having reported a problem
  • Fixed focus view keeping a finished reply hidden while a Stop hook was running
  • Fixed Claude getting a long managed PostToolUse hook output twice when a mod added context to the tool call
  • Fixed /model listing the wrong models in some terminal sessions when a project's .claude/settings.json sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to an LLM gateway
  • Fixed /statusline writing to ~/.claude/settings.json when CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR points to another folder
  • Fixed claudeMdExcludes patterns on Windows not matching a path whose drive letter is written in the other case
  • Fixed claude agents and claude rm refusing to remove a fully pushed session ("The worktree has unpushed commits") when its worktree has a file or folder named HEAD at the top level
  • Fixed long ListAgents results hiding most sessions on accounts with many cloud or Remote Control sessions: long lists now come in pages
  • Fixed slow turns in resumed sessions for organizations with tens of thousands of connector tool permissions
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed claude -p started by a session's script or hook waiting out rate limits, because it inherited the session's own retry setting
  • Fixed the spend limit menu reporting a changed limit when the server refused it
  • Fixed a second x on a task's details in /tasks stopping the next task too
  • Fixed Esc being ignored on a permission prompt that had just appeared
  • Fixed lists that load their rows late sometimes ignoring Enter and the arrow keys
  • Fixed /autofix-pr holding the keyboard after Esc while it stopped the cloud session; the dialog now closes at once, and a stop that fails is reported afterwards with a link
  • Fixed a blank screen and stray mouse codes in the shell after quitting with ctrl+c just after ← opens the agents view
  • Fixed Ctrl+C right after the trust question leaving the terminal in fullscreen
  • Fixed the shell flashing on screen when ← opens the agents view in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed terminal display faults: most scrambled scrollback in Ghostty on resize, link addresses hidden in Windows Terminal under old tmux and in VTE 0.50.0, and no selection highlight with 16 colors
  • Fixed some garbled rows in tmux with allow-passthrough on inside kitty, Ghostty or iTerm2
  • Fixed /mcp saying no servers were configured after one was added during a session or declined; it now says what to do
  • Fixed /hooks leaving out hooks given by --settings
  • Fixed the / menu listing a row for each skill of the same name, though every row ran the first
  • Fixed /teleport showing no message when the chosen session failed to resume
  • Fixed n and N in transcript search skipping matches
  • Fixed cancelling a transcript search (ctrl+o, then /) in a long session landing far from where the search started
  • Fixed up and down losing the cursor's column over a short or blank line
  • Fixed Tab in shell mode filling in a file name after &&, ; or |, where a command goes
  • Fixed the selected session leaving the screen in claude --resume and /resume when branch names or folder paths are long
  • Fixed the MCP tool list in /mcp and /plugin losing your place when going back from a tool
  • Fixed /resume listing one session fewer than the window has room for, and a 'Resend your message' hint after most spend caps, where resending can't help
  • Fixed an MCP server's long question being cut off after one row, text fields hiding long pastes with no sign, and a doubled divider line in /plugin's options and /login's Bedrock and Vertex steps
  • Fixed the "+N lines" count being too high for command output with links or colors, and the transcript's ? help hiding how to exit in a short window
  • Fixed Ctrl+C twice not closing /chrome from its browser list
  • Fixed a number and Enter typed too early at an agent's plan approval in screen reader mode causing the next number to be dropped too
  • Fixed Claude trying to read design system token files that do not exist when starting a deck or design
  • Fixed exit not saying that a worktree was kept
  • Fixed /hooks help naming input fields that do not exist
  • Fixed question dialogs naming ctrl+g after the external editor key was rebound
  • Fixed two sign-in error messages that pointed to the Claude subscription option on computers where forceLoginMethod is set to console
  • Fixed /config saying the dialog was dismissed instead of "Set theme to …" after changing the theme
  • Bug fixes and reliability improvements
  • Improved the speed of a session's first Bash command: shell start-up files may now run before it's approved, even if it's refused; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_SHELL_HEAD_START=1 to turn this off
  • Improved commits on newer models and in PowerShell: Claude is now told not to commit files that likely contain secrets
  • Improved sandboxed shell commands: Claude now sees when a command exempt from the sandbox stayed in it because its permission check relied on the sandbox
  • Improved the refusal for shell commands with no rm that the dangerous rm check can't parse, so Claude can resend harmless ones in plain syntax instead of giving up
  • Improved resuming very long sessions: a transcript read that ends early is now retried once, so messages are lost less often
  • Improved subagent answers that hit the output token limit twice: they now more often come back whole or say up front that they are partial
  • Improved long replies on unrecognized models: a reply cut at 32,000 output tokens now continues with a limit of 128,000
  • Improved the reminder about a completed subagent after compaction: if Claude can't read the agent's output file, it is now told to ask the agent with SendMessage
  • Improved the warning shown when an API key and an Anthropic profile are both set: it now says which one is in use and how to switch to the profile
  • Improved /plugin: the question before removing a marketplace now says that its plugins' settings and saved data are deleted, and a marketplace's page no longer shows another marketplace's error
  • Windows: Improved start-up time with no Git Bash and no pwsh on PATH by checking PowerShell's standard install locations at once; System32's powershell.exe now wins over one earlier on PATH
  • Improved startup time on Windows when PATH points to Git for Windows' bin folder, by starting git.exe directly instead of through its launcher
  • Windows: Improved PowerShell tool speed by up to about half a second per command
  • Improved how soon the Bash tool's diff of changed files is ready in auto and bypass permissions modes
  • Improved speed of the Bash permission check on very deeply nested missing paths on macOS and Linux, and of secret masking on very long text with a URL
  • Improved transcript search to find text in edits and written files
  • Improved speed of reading large PNG images, and the quality of the JPEG sent in their place
  • Improved the Artifact tool to read an uploaded file by the address the artifact's page shows; other forms still fail, most with a message that says to read uploads one per call, by id
  • Improved the Artifact tool to ignore prompt, limit and label on some calls that do not use them instead of failing the call
  • Improved MCP server pages in /mcp: local, remote and agent servers share one layout, menus end in Back, and actions are no longer numbered outside screen reader mode; use the arrow keys and Enter
  • Improved narrow terminals: /status, forms and detail screens lay out better, /model and /effort fit at about 40 columns, and key hints such as ←/→ to adjust stay
  • Improved /install-github-app: the repository, secret and API key steps use the standard list and keys, with shorter messages, a spinner and clearer errors
  • Improved /desktop: the download question is a standard list instead of y/n
  • Changed ExitWorktree to ask before removing a worktree that may hold unsaved work; refused in don't-ask mode or with nobody to answer, unless an allow rule, auto or bypass permissions mode allows it
  • Changed claude mcp add --scope project to stop, instead of overwriting the file, when .mcp.json lists its servers at the top level with no mcpServers key
  • Changed the arrow keys on most permission prompts to stop at No instead of wrapping around; a number past the last answer moves to No
  • Changed path checks to refuse some symbolic links
  • Changed what counts as inside a working directory, so some paths now ask for permission
  • Changed permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories to ask about more Bash commands in bypass and auto modes, and to deny some in auto mode
  • Changed permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories to refuse more Bash commands that name a path under a Read or Edit deny rule, where it used to ask
  • Changed auto mode's notice about falling back to billed classifier requests to say that an upcoming release removes the fallback; each action it would have checked will be asked about or denied
  • Changed auto mode to ignore more allow rules that run any package, like Bash(pnpm dlx *), and path or version forms of ones it already ignored (/usr/bin/npm run:*); the safety check decides those
  • Changed /sandbox and most /config value lists to be unnumbered outside screen reader mode; use the arrow keys and Enter
  • Changed Bash commands whose variables expand to very long text to be denied, with a message that says to use shorter values or a file
  • Changed the PowerShell tool to ask before one more command, even under a rule naming it; if nothing answers, it's refused unless a whole-tool rule, auto mode or bypass permissions mode allows it
  • Changed a subagent resumed by a sibling's message to follow the session's permission settings; it may now ask, or be refused where nobody can answer
  • Changed --worktree with a relative --add-dir beside the launch folder to give the Bash sandbox that folder, not one beside the worktree
  • Changed some --worktree starts with a relative --add-dir above the launch folder, such as .., to give the Bash sandbox, and a --bg session, only the worktree
  • Changed Claude in Chrome to refuse uploading some credential files; attach those to the page yourself
  • Changed artifact approval in organizations that require it for each new artifact: an artifact that only a plugin created or allowed can be refused
  • Changed sessions with nobody to ask to refuse a new artifact at once, with no permission prompt, in organizations that require approval of each one
  • Changed the Artifact tool to refuse calls once settings turn Artifacts off, in sessions already running too
  • Changed the Artifact publish prompt to stop offering "don't ask again" in subagents and after a background task result, someone else's message or a compaction
  • Changed claude plugin eval to keep its deny rules over a plugin's permission hook, and to flag calls the hook let through
  • Changed MCP server logs to record the mode, action, and field names of elicitation requests and hook answers, not their full contents
  • Changed most prompts to ignore answers other than Esc for a moment after resuming with fg
  • Changed Code Mode to no longer refuse to start when an installed mod hooks tool calls; an administrator can still keep Code Mode off in managed settings
  • Changed subagents launched without a model to stay on the model they started on when resumed, including after /model
  • Changed the first subagent on a model to wait up to 1.5 seconds (10 in claude -p) for that model's settings from Anthropic, instead of starting without them
  • Changed restarted background subagents, and turns that start by themselves, to wait for plugins to load
  • Changed prompt history to leave out most launch prompts of sessions that another Claude Code session started, such as claude --bg run by Claude
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions on Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI and Microsoft Foundry to be written from short notes, not the whole conversation, using far fewer tokens
  • Changed non-interactive (-p) mode to run fewer git commands before the first request
  • Changed first-run setup to skip terminal setup in remote VS Code, Cursor and Devin Desktop sessions, where it cannot change settings
  • Changed fullscreen text selection to leave out the glyph of system, thinking and inbound message lines
  • Changed Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions to ignore more of a repository's flag and plugin delivery settings; its CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC now acts at most as DISABLE_TELEMETRY
  • [VSCode] Added "Claude Code: Add to Chat" to the Explorer's right-click menu, which @-mentions the selected files and folders in the chat
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt not showing the reason that a PreToolUse hook gives when it asks for confirmation (#85950)
  • [VSCode] Fixed long tool and file names being cut off in a permission prompt's title
  • [VSCode] Fixed a terminal session's diff showing the previous proposed edit after you typed in it and Claude edited the same file again
  • [VSCode] Fixed Escape also stopping Claude's response when it closes the feedback or "Build a custom style" dialog, the @-mention menu, the model, mode or "+" menu, or another popup
  • [VSCode] Improved speed when Claude makes several edits in a row: queued edits share one wait for new problems; a problem may be reported with a later edit
  • [VSCode] Improved @-mention file search speed in large workspaces when rg is on your PATH; results now rank much as in the terminal, with less tolerance for typos
  • [VSCode] Improved startup: the model picker is ready at once in folders opened for the first time, empty windows and worktrees, except on third-party providers
  • [VSCode] Changed a chat edit's diff to stay open and keep asking for approval when a terminal session in the same window sends a prompt
  • [VSCode] Removed unused tools from the IDE connection (openFile, saveDocument, getOpenEditors and related)

items.title: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on Vera Rubin NVL72: 58x Throughput vs. GB300 NVL72 at 387 tokens/s
items.summary: On one NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 rack, vLLM serves DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on SemiAnalysis AgentX at 1.7M tokens/s per GPU at a P90 of 387 tokens/s per user, 58x GB300 NVL72 at the same interactivity.

The gains come from building on what is new in Rubin: kernels tuned for its split memory and FP4 tensor cores, specialized decode kernels for low latency, and a rack-wide KV cache and Engram tables shared over NVLink. This is the third post in our DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash series. The first post covered day-0 bring-up and kernel fusions. The second scaled the model to a GB300 NVL72 rack with P/D disaggregation and Wide-EP. This post moves the same stack to Vera Rubin NVL72, which we introduced last month . Rubin opens up new avenues for optimization. We start with the hardware facts that shaped our work, then go through four groups of optimizations: Figure 1: SemiAnalysis AgentX on NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 (vLLM, P/D disaggregation, Wide-EP) vs. GB300 NVL72. Throughput counts cached input, uncached input and output tokens ( GB300 source ). We measure performance with the SemiAnalysis AgentX benchmark as a representative agentic serving workload, aligned with our previous posts. Figure 1 compares the two racks' raw throughput (total tokens per GPU per second, including input, cached, and output) and power-normalized throughput, respectively in two tabs. We use the same methodology as in our previous GB300 post . For kernels and model forward profiling, vllm bench forward times exact prefill and decode batches through the real execute_model path, with real weights and real AgentX tokens. We A/B prefill kernels in loops that run for several seconds and report sustained numbers where they differ. Three properties of Vera Rubin NVL72 drove most of the decisions below. Where an optimization is specific to Rubin, we say which of them it relies on. Figure 2: Weight stages of the routed-expert GEMM in one SM's shared memory, with the SM100 MXFP8×MXFP4 MMA and with SM107's K64 MXFP8×MXFP4 MMA on packed FP4. We kept GB300's three engine shapes: DEP2 prefill, Wide-EP decode (DEP16 or DEP32), and a TP decode path for the lowest latency (next section). items.story_key: story|title:introducing alphaproof code a breakthrough in verifying complex software at dept
items.content_excerpt: How Google DeepMind researchers built a new agentic framework that formally verified the code of Signal’s cryptographic protocol — long considered to be a grand security challenge Today, we’re sharing a milestone in software security long considered to be a grand challenge: Google DeepMind researchers guided AI agents to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code underlying the Signal protocol, the technology that protects billions of private conversations in apps like Signal and Google Messages. This breakthrough discovery was made using AlphaProof Code , a novel agentic framework for formal verification at unprecedented depth that combines human expertise with AI agents. Formal verification—mathematically proving code runs correctly without flaws—is the highest standard of security assurance; however, it is difficult and often labor-intensive. Our work marks the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth. It's also the first time the implementation of a widely deployed protocol like this has been formally verified by any method, with or without AI. AlphaProof Code is a multi-LLM agentic framework that splits the work of formal verification the way a research team would: human experts work with AI to decide what to prove, and a group of AI agents does it. First, our researchers collaborated with a mix of models to translate Signal’s security goals into formal mathematical specifications, with human experts reviewing every one. From there, agents powered by Gemini Carbon did the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language that mathematically proves the accuracy of code. Next, the agents audited the proof and highlighted areas that needed a second look by a human – just one percent of the codebase, a massive time savings. Because Lean automatically checks the rest, our experts could focus their review where human judgment matters most. Cryptographic protocols underpin nearly all digital communication, from online banking to web browsing, and a single flaw can expose millions of people at once. That's why experts have spent decades formally analyzing them. But most protocol verification stops at the design level. Our agents went further, proving that the compiled code fulfills the key security properties – such as keeping messages protected before and after a device is temporarily compromised – down to the exact code running on devices. items.content_excerpt: The scope of tasks that agents can take on has increased drastically over the past few years. They have gone from simple text generation to tool calling and decision making to executing full tasks. The future of agents is them taking on open ended goals and driving towards completion of those goals. Launches like that of Hone give us a glimpse into that future. In this world, designing the scope of agents is crucial. Point them in the wrong direction, and you’ll get a lot of wasted tokens. A key part of the Hone agent set up is defining metrics for them to optimize. As we’ve worked on similar styles of agents, we’ve realized something about designing the scope for agents: you want to design the scope of an agent such that it makes it as easy as possible to give feedback as the agent operates within that scope. When agents mess up, a big reason they mess up is lack of right context. In order to fix this, you need to give the agent the right context. There are different types of context. Some types of context are things like access to the right documents or APIs - that is relatively easy to fix. The trickiest context to give the agent is context that is not written down anywhere already. This context needs to be given to the agent as feedback from a human expert. This is especially important as agents expand beyond doing verifiable tasks and start taking on subjective work alongside humans within an organization. For example, if you want an agent to help optimize a business metric (like improving your ads to optimize marketing performance), there are so many nuances beyond just factual context that you want to govern how the agent behaves. You probably have a certain taste around what sounds and looks good. You have opinions about how provocative or out-there your brand can be. An agent that can’t effectively get feedback to learn these things quickly becomes useless. If the scope of your agent makes it really easy to give lots of high quality feedback on the agent’s work, that will help you immensely in building an agent that can reliably pursue a long-horizon goal. A related learning is that you want to invest a lot in an intuitive and delightful UX for reviewing agent work. The bottleneck for agents performing is often them learning from feedback. Therefore, you should seek to optimize ease and quality of feedback collection! Investing in a clear UX for that is a worthwhile investment. items.summary:
Release: llm-gemini 0.37

Google launched Gemini 4 Hydrogen today - the lowest cost member of the Gemini 4 family.

It's actually not too far off the price of its much bigger siblings, Carbon and Argon. I'm finding Gemini 4's pricing really confusing. Here's the pricing scheme:

Model Dates Input ($/M) Cached input Output
Gemini 4 Carbon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Argon Through Nov 30, 2026 $2.00 $0.10 $10.00
From Dec 1, 2026 $4.00 $0.20 $20.00
Gemini 4 Hydrogen   $1.50 $0.075 $7.50

Carbon and Argon are the same price, and both are scheduled to double in price on December 1st. If they're the same price, why have two different models? Google says that Argon "delivers Gemini 4 intelligence with faster responses and lower token spend per turn compared to Gemini 4 Carbon" - so it may be priced the same, but it will use less tokens per task.

Hydrogen, supposedly the cheap model, is currently only a 25% discount on its more capable peers. The Hydrogen price will make more sense after December 1st, when it will represent a 75% discount. It's still considerably more expensive than Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna - they're both $0.10/$0.50, so Hydrogen is 15x that.

I had Hydrogen generate some pelicans. Here's a full comparison grid showing the pelicans for all three members of the Gemini 4 family at their three supported effort levels:

Considering how close they are in price, the difference in pelican quality for Hydrogen is quite stark.

Here's how Google describe Hydrogen's intended position in their mix of models:

In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows.

Most notably, Hydrogen is the new free tier model, and is the model that will power AI features in Google Search.
